extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and researchers studying algebraic geometry (e.g., readers of Vakil's 'The Rising Sea')
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes the textbook's criteria, definitions, and theorems about representability of parameter spaces (Grassmannian, hypersurfaces), completion, singularity definitions, the Theorem on Formal Functions, and related results (Zariski connectedness, Stein factorization).

rubrics_metrics.name: Representability of G'(k,n) by G(k,n) (Theorem 28.3.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: The functor G'(k,n) (from Schemes to Sets) assigning to a scheme B the set of finitely presented closed subschemes X ⊂ P^{n-1}_B, flat over B, whose fiber over any point b is a linearly embedded P^{k-1}_{κ(b)}, is represented by G(k,n). Translation: there is a natural bijection between diagrams of the form (28.3.3.1) (fibers P^{k-1}) and diagrams of the form (16.7.0.1) that G(k,n) parametrizes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One direction uses: given O_B^n ↠ Q (Q locally free rank k) apply Proj_B to Sym• and obtain a closed embedding Proj_B(Sym• Q) ↪ P^{n-1}_B whose fibers are linearly embedded P^{k-1}; the reverse construction uses cohomology and base change to produce the locally free quotient from a family of embedded P^{k-1}'s. See diagrams (28.3.3.1), (28.3.4.1), (28.3.4.2) and the exercises 28.3.C–E for details and verification that the constructions are inverse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction via Proj(Sym•) producing embedded projective bundles
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying Proj_B to Sym• applied to a locally free quotient Q of O_B^n yields Proj_B(Sym• Q) which is flat, finitely presented over B and embeds as a family of linearly embedded P^{k-1}'s in P^{n-1}_B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to show one direction of representability of G'(k,n). Fibers being P^{k-1} follows since Proj commutes with base change; Proj(Sym• Q) is a projective bundle hence flat and finitely presented (see Exercise 17.2.H and 17.2.E).

rubrics_metrics.name: Riπ_* OX(1) is locally free of rank k (Exercise 28.3.C)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a family π:X→B whose fibers are P^{k-1}'s linearly embedded in P^{n-1}_B, Riπ_* OX(1) = 0 for i>0 and π_* OX(1) is locally free of rank k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hint: use the Cohomology and Base Change Theorem 28.1.6 and vanishing of higher cohomology of O(1) on P^{k-1} (see §18.3). Either assume B locally Noetherian or use non-Noetherian discussion (or use 28.2.9 if available). This is a key step in recovering a rank-k locally free quotient from the geometric family.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short exact sequence of locally free sheaves from pushforwards (Exercise 28.3.D)
rubrics_metrics.description: From the closed subscheme exact sequence 0 → I_X → O_{P^{n-1}_B} → O_X → 0, after twisting by O(1) and applying π_*, the long exact sequence becomes a short exact sequence 0 → π_* I_X(1) → π_* O_{P^{n-1}_B}(1) → π_* O_X(1) → 0 of locally free sheaves of ranks n-k, n, and k respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The middle term π_* O_{P^{n-1}_B}(1) is canonically O_B^n. The surjection O_B^n = π_*O_{P^{n-1}_B}(1) → π_* O_X(1) is precisely the locally free quotient diagram (16.7.0.1) needed for representability. Use cohomology and base change and the vanishing of higher pushforwards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representability of Hd,n by projective space (Proposition 28.3.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define the contravariant functor H_{d,n} assigning to a scheme B the set of closed subschemes X ⊂ P^n_B, flat and finitely presented over B, whose fibers are degree d hypersurfaces. Then H_{d,n} is represented by P^{(n+d choose d)-1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One direction: the universal hypersurface X ⊂ P^n × P^{(n+d choose d)-1} gives a flat finitely presented family; reverse: from a family X→B use the exact sequence 0 → I_X(d) → O_{P^n_B}(d) → O_X(d) → 0 and cohomology and base change to identify π_* O_{P^n_B}(d) with a free sheaf whose summands correspond to monomials of degree d. Then π_* I_X(d) is locally free rank 1 (a line bundle) and dualizing the injection gives a surjection from the free sheaf to an invertible sheaf, hence a morphism B → P^{(n+d choose d)-1}. See Exercises 28.3.F and 28.3.H and 28.3.A for base change remarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dualizing the rank-1 subsheaf yields the classifying morphism (hypersurface case)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given the injection π_* I_X(d) ↪ O_B^{(n+d choose d)}, dualizing gives a surjection O_B^{(n+d choose d)} ↠ L where L is invertible; by the universal property of projective space this produces the morphism B → P^{(n+d choose d)-1} classifying the hypersurface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret π_* I_X(d) as 'the equation of X' (a rank 1 subsheaf of the free sheaf of degree-d monomials), then dualize and apply the projective universal property; close the loop by showing the two constructions are inverses (Exercise 28.3.H).

rubrics_metrics.name: Completion and I-adic completion (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a ring A and a decreasing sequence of ideals J_1 ⊃ J_2 ⊃ ⋯, the limit lim← A/J_n is the completion (often denoted ^A). The most important case is J_n = I^n (I-adic completion); ^A is the I-adic completion of A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: k[[x_1,…,x_n]] is the completion of k[x_1,…,x_n] at the maximal ideal (x_1,…,x_n); p-adic numbers are another example. Cofinal sequences give canonically isomorphic completions (Exercise 29.2.A). The completion has a natural topology (inverse limit of discrete quotients) making it a topological ring; modules over it can be given compatible topologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topological ring/module structure and I-adic separation (29.2.2 remarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: With the discrete topology on the quotients A/J_n, the inverse limit ^A is a topological ring; a topological module M over ^A is an underlying module with a topology making the action continuous. If A → ^A is injective, A is I-adically separated or complete with respect to I.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Krull Intersection Theorem for Noetherian domains/local rings to see injectivity in many cases. This viewpoint motivates interpreting completions as 'formal neighborhoods' and working with topological properties when discussing formal-local behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cohen-structure-type surjection k[[t_1,…,t_n]] → ^A (Exercises 29.2.C/D)
rubrics_metrics.description: If (A,m) is a Noetherian local k-algebra of dimension d and x_1,…,x_n map to a basis of m/m^2, then the natural map k[[t_1,…,t_n]] → ^A sending t_i ↦ x_i is surjective (special case of Cohen Structure Theorem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 29.2.D uses this to identify completions ^O_{X,p} ≅ k[[x_1,…,x_d]] when p is a regular k-valued point of a k-variety. The map is constructed by lifting generators of m/m^2 and checking surjectivity; see Atkinson-Macdonald references for the general theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Étale morphisms induce isomorphisms on completions (Exercises 29.2.E/F)
rubrics_metrics.description: If π:X→Y is étale at p with π(p)=q and induces an isomorphism of residue fields, then π induces an isomorphism of completions ^O_{Y,q} ≅ ^O_{X,p}. More generally, étale morphisms induce isomorphisms of formal neighborhoods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: the implicit function theorem holds formally locally for étale maps. The exercises guide through explicit cases like X = Spec A[t]/(f(t)) and use Hensel-type arguments; this motivates the idea that although étale maps need not be Zariski-local isomorphisms, they are formal-local isomorphisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 29.2.6: completion flatness and exactness (Noetherian case)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose A is Noetherian and I ⊂ A. (a) The completion ^A (I-adic) is flat over A. (b) If M is finitely generated then the natural map ^A ⊗_A M → ^M is an isomorphism. (c) If 0 → M → N → P → 0 is short exact with finitely generated modules, then 0 → ^M → ^N → ^P → 0 is exact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof strategy: prove (c) via exercises (use inverse limits and surjectivity of transition maps), then deduce (b) and (a). Uses Artin–Rees lemma (Exercise 12.9.3) and the ideal-theoretic criterion for flatness (Theorem 24.4.1). Warning/caveat: completion need not be exact on arbitrary (non-finitely generated) modules — see provided counterexample with infinite direct sums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stronger ideal-theoretic criterion for flatness (Exercise 29.2.J)
rubrics_metrics.description: An A-module M is flat iff for all finitely generated ideals I the natural map I ⊗_A M → M is injective (i.e., the usual ideal-theoretic criterion can be tested on finitely generated ideals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to reduce flatness checks to finitely generated ideals; it's used in the proof that the completion ^A is flat by checking that ^A ⊗_A I → ^A is injective for finitely generated I and using part (c) of Theorem 29.2.6.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of node via completion (Definition 29.3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let X be a variety over a field k and p a closed point. X has a node at p if the completion ^O_{X,p} (at the maximal ideal) is isomorphic as a topological ring to k[[x,y]]/(xy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises 29.3.A/B show examples and give algebraic criteria for nodes in affine curves (degree-2 part not a perfect square etc.). Over non-algebraically closed fields one may define split nodes (when p is k-valued and completion is k[[x,y]]/(xy)) vs non-split nodes which become nodes after base change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of cusp, tacnode, triple point, ordinary m-fold point via completion (29.3.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a closed point p on a curve over an algebraically closed field k: cusp if ^O_{X,p} ≅ completion of k[x,y]/(y^2 - x^3); tacnode if y^2 - x^4; triple point if y^3 - x^3; ordinary m-fold point if completion ≅ k[x,y]/(f) with f homogeneous degree m with no repeated roots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These definitions generalize the node notion; exercises ask to define A_n singularities and D_n, E_6, E_7, E_8 surface/curve singularities and relate δ-invariant (contribution to arithmetic genus) to resolving singularities (δ=1 for node/cusp, δ=2 for tacnode).

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem on Formal Functions (Theorem 29.4.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose π:X→Y is a proper morphism of locally Noetherian schemes and F is a coherent sheaf on X. For q ∈ Y closed, the natural map Riπ_* F ^_q → lim← H^i(X_n, F|_{X_n}) (where X_n are the n-th infinitesimal neighborhoods of the fiber over q) is an isomorphism for all i ≥ 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Setup: identify Riπ_*F ^_q with the completion of Hi(X_B, F|_{X_B}) at the maximal ideal m_B for an affine neighborhood Spec B of q, construct base change maps Hi(X_{n+1},F) → Hi(X_n,F) compatible with quotient maps Hi(X_B,F)/m^n, then take limits to get the map (29.4.1.2). Warning: the theorem does NOT assert anything about the finite-level maps Hi(X_{n+1},F) → Hi(X_n,F) themselves — only about the limit and the completion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zariski's Connectedness Lemma (29.5.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If π:X→Y is proper and O-connected (see 28.1.7) then for every q∈Y the fiber π^{-1}(q) is connected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses formal neighborhoods and idempotents: if fiber were disconnected write idempotent functions distinguishing pieces on formal neighborhoods and obtain nontrivial idempotents in the local ring completion ^O_{Y,q}, but the completion is local (Exercise 29.5.A), contradiction. The lemma is used to deduce connectedness of fibers in many situations (e.g., birational morphisms to normal Y).

rubrics_metrics.name: Stein Factorization Theorem (29.5.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any proper morphism π:X→Y of locally Noetherian schemes factors functorially as X —α→ Y' —β→ Y where α is O-connected and β is finite (Y' := Spec π_* O_X). Y' is proper over Y and β finite; α has connected fibers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: set Y' := Spec π_* O_X (π_* O_X is a coherent O_Y-algebra by Grothendieck's Coherence Theorem). Use Zariski Connectedness Lemma to show α is O-connected. Remarks: gives canonical 'contraction' of connected components in fibers; cancellation theorem implies if π projective then α projective; exercises discuss uniqueness, behavior under flat base change, and the birational/normal case (Zariski's Main Theorem for birational morphisms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolution of singularities of curves by normalization and blowing up (29.5.4 and following)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a reduced projective curve C over a field k, normalization ν:˜C→C resolves singularities. Algorithmically one can desingularize by repeatedly blowing up singular points; the process is controlled by the arithmetic genus pa, which decreases when resolving singularities (e.g., resolving a node reduces pa by 1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key facts to check: (i) if pa(C)=pa(˜C) then ν is an isomorphism (so C nonsingular); (ii) for a finite birational morphism π:C'→C, pa(C') ≥ pa(C) with equality iff π is O-connected; (iii) blowing up a singular point decreases pa. Use exact sequences for π_* O_{C'} and support considerations; Exercises 29.5.D and 29.5.E guide the arguments (showing O-connectedness implies isomorphism, etc.).
